abstract: Horton examines how AI agents might reduce transaction costs to near zero, dramatically reshaping labor markets and the boundaries of firms. Drawing on Coase's theory of the firm — which explains firm boundaries as determined by the relative costs of market transactions versus internal coordination — the paper argues that if AI agents can effectively act as economic agents (hiring, contracting, negotiating, monitoring), the traditional justifications for firm boundaries dissolve. In this 'Coasean Singularity' scenario, labor markets become radically more fluid, with AI agents enabling real-time matching of tasks to workers, continuous renegotiation of contracts, and near-frictionless coordination across organizational boundaries. The paper explores implications for employment relationships, worker bargaining power, and market design, suggesting that the emergence of AI agents as market intermediaries could be more consequential for labor markets than AI's direct substitution for human tasks.
keyFindings: If AI agents reduce transaction costs to near zero, the traditional Coasean rationale for firm boundaries dissolves, enabling radically more fluid labor markets with continuous task-level matching.
AI agents acting as economic intermediaries — hiring, contracting, negotiating, monitoring — could reshape labor markets more fundamentally than AI's direct substitution for human tasks.
Near-zero transaction costs would enable firms to disaggregate work into smaller task units, matched and coordinated in real time by AI agents rather than managed through employment relationships.

Worker bargaining power could shift dramatically in either direction: AI agents might empower workers through better matching and reduced information asymmetries, or disempower them through employer-side automation of management and negotiation.

Market design becomes critical — the institutional structures governing AI-mediated labor markets will determine whether the Coasean Singularity benefits workers or concentrates gains among platform owners and AI-equipped firms.
methodology: Theoretical analysis building on Coase's theory of the firm, extending transaction cost economics to incorporate AI agents as market participants. The paper develops conceptual models of how AI-mediated transaction cost reduction affects firm boundaries, employment relationships, and labor market structure. The framework draws on platform economics, market design theory, and emerging evidence on AI agent capabilities.
qualifiers: Primarily theoretical and speculative — the Coasean Singularity scenario assumes AI agents achieve capabilities (autonomous negotiation, contracting, quality assessment) that remain far from current reality. The paper presents a limiting case rather than a near-term prediction. Transaction costs include trust, relationship-specific investment, and tacit knowledge that may resist AI-mediated reduction. Legal and regulatory frameworks for AI agent economic activity remain undeveloped, potentially constraining the described transformation.
